name: combustion-reports
oneLiner: A car's fuel consumption as a curve rather than two numbers from a brochure — with a README section on how **not** to read that curve.
summary: The manufacturer quotes two numbers, city and highway; the car has a curve. The application takes recorded trips and fits a polynomial model of consumption against average speed and against route length, so you can see where a car is genuinely efficient rather than where the brochure says it is. It runs entirely in the browser: no account, no server, no telemetry, state in `localStorage`. What sets this repository apart from everything else in the portfolio is its **'How not to read it'** section — a curve fitted to four points is a drawing, not a model; the fit is anchored at the origin by default, which is not physically true and is a stability trade-off; extrapolation is deliberately short, to 1.2× the furthest sample; and the largest confound is the driver's own right foot. R² is displayed next to every fit precisely so that it can be disbelieved. That is rare: a product that actively makes it harder to over-read its own output.
tests: Five Vitest test files, focused on the polynomial fit and the persistence layer. The storage tests cover the cases applications like this usually break on: an incompatible schema version, a corrupt entry, no access to `localStorage` at all.
ci: Two workflows: `ci.yml` (lint and tests) and `pages.yml`, which publishes the application. A Docker image with nginx is built but published nowhere.

metrics.label: Interface languages
metrics.value: 2 — English and Polish, detected from the browser

components.name: The polynomial fit
components.description: A degree-2 fit, anchored at the origin by default. The anchor is not physically true — an idling car still burns fuel — but without it a handful of samples produces a curve that swings wildly outside the data. The trade-off is documented and can be switched off with a parameter.

components.name: The persistence layer
components.description: Writes are debounced, the snapshot carries a schema version, and a snapshot from an incompatible version is discarded rather than half-loaded. When `localStorage` is unavailable or full, the application keeps working in memory instead of throwing.

components.name: The 'How not to read it' section
components.description: Four warnings against over-reading, written by the author against his own product: too few points, the origin anchor, the short extrapolation, and the driver's own habits as a confound.

components.name: The bilingual interface
components.description: English and Polish, switchable from the navigation bar and detected from the browser on the first visit — exactly the arrangement the portfolio map uses, solved independently.

overlaps.reason: The same species: a calculator that computes entirely in the browser, with no account and no backend, and a model written out so it can be checked. The persistence layer and the state-sharing pattern are common to both and have never been extracted.
A browser application holding all its state locally on the user's machine, with the same set of problems: schema versioning, no export, data migration between releases.

product: The closest thing to a product among the things built for their own sake: it solves a real problem, has an audience beyond the author, and needs no infrastructure, so the marginal cost per user is zero. What it lacks to be a product is not features but data export — without it a user who has entered a hundred trips is tied to one browser on one machine.
highlights: A section on how **not** to read its own output. In a portfolio full of repositories honestly listing their own gaps, this is the cleanest case of that same virtue aimed at the user rather than at a reviewer.
R² shown next to every fit — shown, not hidden. The application hands the reader the number that lets them disbelieve it.
The origin anchor is a documented trade-off with a rationale and an escape hatch rather than a hidden implementation decision. Most tools in this class make that decision and never mention it.
The persistence layer degrades correctly: private browsing, blocked cookies and an exceeded quota do not take the application down, they switch it to memory.
gaps: **No export.** All state sits in one browser's `localStorage`: clearing site data destroys everything, and moving to another device is impossible. It is the single thing standing between this application and being useful to a stranger.
The last substantive commit is from 1 August 2026; since then the only things open have been Dependabot pull requests.
The Docker image is built and published nowhere — configuration that does nothing except require maintenance.
next: Add JSON export and import. It is one feature, and it decides whether anyone but the author will ever record a hundred trips in this application.
Merge the two Dependabot pull requests and decide whether the repository is maintained or frozen — today the badge says one thing and the commit history another.
Publish the image to GHCR or delete the Dockerfile and `nginx.conf`. An unused deployment path is a cost with no benefit.
risks: User data lives in one browser only and cannot be exported. A user who has been entering trips for a year will lose them on a site-data clear — with no warning at all.
headline: It has a section on how not to read its own charts — and no way to export your data
